key_terms.meaning: Augmented reality: real world seen directly, with computer-generated content overlaid and registered to it.
Mostly virtual world with some real content, such as a live camera feed, inserted into it.
VR setup that blocks most of the real world, usually a head-mounted display or a CAVE.
Mixed reality: real and virtual content coexist, are anchored to each other, and interact in real time.
VR shown on an ordinary monitor with keyboard or mouse; low sensory surround.
VR using a large screen or projection wall; some surround, but the real room is still visible.
Virtual reality: a computer-generated environment that replaces the real world for the user's senses.
Extended reality: umbrella term covering VR, AR, MR and augmented virtuality.
Informal ranking of VR setups from non-immersive to semi-immersive to fully immersive.
Line from real environment to virtual environment, with AR and augmented virtuality in between.
Computer-generated 3D world with objects, rules and a user viewpoint.
Extent to which a system surrounds the senses and blocks real-world signals.
User's ability to act in the virtual world and receive a timely response.
Ability of the content and design to engage the user's mind and make the scenario believable.
Sensor system that measures an object's position and orientation over time.
Glove with sensors that measure finger bend and hand pose for gesture input.
Device that applies force, vibration or temperature to give touch feedback.
Software that draws each frame from the scene model and current viewpoint.
Software that updates world state, physics, object behaviour and rules over time.
Stored scene database of geometry, materials, lights and object states.

takeaways: VR, AR, MR and XR are four mixes of real and computer-generated content, not four unrelated technologies.
The reality–virtuality continuum runs from the real environment to a fully virtual environment, with AR and augmented virtuality in between.
VR history is best remembered as three waves: early stereo and simulator work, the 1980s–90s laboratory era, and the 2010s consumer wave.
Every VR experience is judged on immersion, interaction and imagination; one weak element spoils the whole experience.
3D computer graphics produces a picture chosen by the animator, while VR produces a picture chosen by the user's head and hands in real time.
A VR system has four parts: input devices, output devices, a computer running the world model and simulation, and the human user.
VR, AR and MR differ on how much real world reaches the eye, whether the system knows where the real world is, and whether virtual content is anchored to real objects.
VR benefits include safe training, clear visualization of complex data, remote collaboration and repeatable practice.
bank_note: The unit's long answers usually ask for definitions on the reality–virtuality continuum, the three I's, the four-part VR system, input and output devices, and a clear comparison of AR, VR and MR.

bank.q: Define VR, AR, MR and XR. Explain the reality–virtuality continuum and place each term on it with one example.
outline: Define each term in one clear sentence.
Draw the continuum from real environment to virtual environment.
Place AR near the real end and augmented virtuality near the virtual end.
Explain that XR is the umbrella term.
Give one Indian-context example for each mix.

bank.q: Explain the three I's of virtual reality: immersion, interaction and imagination. Why does a weak element spoil the experience?
outline: Define immersion, interaction and imagination.
Give one design example for each.
Explain how weak tracking spoils interaction.
Explain how poor content spoils imagination.
Explain how an open room spoils immersion.

bank.q: Compare VR with 3D computer graphics. State the main benefits of VR over a pre-rendered 3D animation.
outline: Define 3D computer graphics as a fixed or pre-chosen viewpoint.
Define VR as a real-time loop driven by head and hand pose.
Explain latency and frame rate requirements.
List benefits such as training, visualization and remote presence.
Give one example where pre-rendering is enough and one where VR is needed.

bank.q: Describe the four components of a VR system: input devices, output devices, the computer and the human user.
outline: Name the four parts.
Input: trackers, gloves, gesture and navigation interfaces.
Output: graphics, sound and haptic displays.
Computer: world model, simulation engine and rendering engine.
Human: visual, auditory and touch senses with their limits.

bank.q: Outline the historical development of VR in three waves. Mention the main technical ideas of each wave.
outline: First wave: stereo views and simulator experiments.
Second wave: laboratory systems in the 1980s–90s that named virtual reality.
Third wave: consumer head-mounted displays from the 2010s.
Link each wave to displays, tracking and cost.
State one scientific landmark for each wave.

bank.q: You must design a VR training module for factory workers on a dangerous machine. Choose the level of immersion, input devices, output displays and safety features. Justify each choice.
outline: Choose fully immersive VR and justify safe practice.
Select 3D position trackers and hand input.
Select graphics and haptic output for machine feel.
Include a supervised stop and a real-world safety boundary.
Explain how the three I's are met.

bank.q: A museum wants a guide for artefacts, a hospital wants surgical rehearsal, and a design team wants remote collaborative product review. Choose AR, VR or MR for each and justify using the three tests.
outline: Museum guide: AR keeps the real gallery visible.
Surgical rehearsal: VR gives a controlled, repeatable virtual body.
Collaborative design: MR or VR depending on shared real objects.
Use real-world visibility, world knowledge and anchoring as tests.
State cost and mobility trade-offs.

bank.q: For a VR cockpit trainer, explain how 3D position trackers, a data glove and gesture input work together to produce interaction.
outline: Trackers measure head and hand pose.
Data glove measures finger bend and grasp.
Gesture input recognises commands such as point or grab.
The simulation engine updates the cockpit state.
Latency and drift must be controlled.

bank.q: Select output devices for a VR classroom lesson on human anatomy. Cover graphics, sound and haptics, and relate each choice to the human visual and auditory systems.
outline: Graphics display: head-mounted display or large screen.
Sound display: spatial audio for guidance.
Haptic display: force feedback for tool use.
Relate field of view and stereo to visual perception.
Relate direction and loudness to auditory perception.

bank.q: “More immersion is always better for a VR application.” Evaluate this statement using the three I's, cost, safety and mobility.
outline: Define immersion and separate it from interaction and imagination.
Show cases where full immersion helps, such as flight training.
Show cases where AR or desktop VR is safer or cheaper.
Discuss motion sickness, isolation and cost.
Conclude that fit to task matters more than maximum immersion.

bank.q: Explain how latency and tracking drift damage interaction in VR. Relate them to the tracking, simulation and rendering parts of the system.
outline: Define latency and tracking drift.
Show how delay between head motion and image update breaks the real-time loop.
Explain how drift causes virtual objects to slide against real ones in AR.
Relate to tracker update rate and rendering frame rate.
Suggest design fixes such as prediction and sensor fusion.

bank.q: Why is real-time computer graphics a requirement for VR? Analyse the roles of the rendering engine, frame rate and scene complexity.
outline: Contrast pre-rendered 3D animation with real-time rendering.
Explain the head-motion-to-photon loop.
Show how low frame rate causes judder and sickness.
Relate scene complexity to rendering cost.
Explain level-of-detail and culling as trade-offs.

bank.q: Compare AR, VR and MR on how much real world reaches the eye, whether the system knows where the real world is, and whether virtual content is anchored to real objects. Recommend one for a collaborative repair task.
outline: Define the three tests clearly.
AR: real world visible, needs tracking, content can be anchored.
VR: real world blocked, no real-world mapping needed.
MR: real and virtual coexist and interact, strong anchoring.
Recommend MR for repair and justify with safety and shared context.

glossary.def: Augmented reality overlays computer-generated content on the directly seen real world.
Virtual reality replaces the user's sensory world with a computer-generated environment.
Mixed reality lets real and virtual objects coexist, anchor to each other and interact in real time.
Extended reality is the umbrella term for VR, AR, MR and augmented virtuality.
A mostly virtual world that includes some real content, such as a live video feed.
A line from the real environment to a fully virtual environment, with mixed forms in between.
A computer-generated 3D world with objects, rules and a user viewpoint.
The extent to which a system surrounds the senses and blocks real-world signals.
The user's ability to act in the virtual world and receive a timely response.
The power of the content and design to engage the user's mind and make the scenario believable.
The user's subjective feeling of being inside the virtual world.
A display worn on the head that shows a separate image to each eye.
A room-sized VR display that projects images on walls to surround the user.
A sensor system that measures position and orientation over time.
The number of independent position and orientation values a tracker measures, commonly three or six.
A glove with sensors that measure finger bend and hand pose.
A device that applies force, vibration or temperature to give touch feedback.
Software that draws each frame from the scene model and current viewpoint.
Software that updates world state, physics, object behaviour and rules over time.
The stored scene database of geometry, materials, lights and object states.
The delay between a user action and the system's response.
The angular extent of the world visible through a display or the eye.
A display that shows slightly different images to the two eyes to create depth.
The feeling of being present at a remote place through sensors and displays.
